concepts.name: Vertices and edges
concepts.summary: Name the parts of a graph and describe a graph as a set of vertices with a set of edges joining pairs of them.

concepts.name: Degree of a vertex
concepts.summary: Compute the degree of each vertex and explain that it counts the edge ends meeting at that vertex.

concepts.name: Directed and undirected edges
concepts.summary: Distinguish edges that can be traversed both ways from arcs with a direction, and draw each kind.

concepts.name: Weighted graphs
concepts.summary: Explain that weights attach numeric costs or distances to edges and read them off a diagram.

concepts.name: Paths and cycles
concepts.summary: Define a path as a sequence of adjacent edges and a cycle as a closed path with no repeated vertices, and identify them in a drawing.

concepts.name: Connectedness
concepts.summary: Decide whether a small graph is connected and identify its connected components.

concepts.name: Handshaking lemma
concepts.summary: State that the sum of degrees equals twice the number of edges and explain why.

misconceptions.text: The way a graph is drawn, including edge lengths and crossings, is part of what the graph is.
A vertex's degree is the number of vertices in the graph.
Edges in a graph always have a direction.

concepts.name: Adjacency matrix representation
concepts.summary: Build the adjacency matrix of a graph and read degrees and edges from it.

concepts.name: Adjacency list representation
concepts.summary: Write an adjacency list for a graph and choose between list and matrix based on graph density.

concepts.name: Breadth-first search
concepts.summary: Trace BFS with a queue on a graph, giving the visiting order and the levels from the start vertex.

concepts.name: Depth-first search
concepts.summary: Trace DFS with a stack or recursion, giving the visiting order and the backtracking steps.

concepts.name: Trees and forests
concepts.summary: Recognise a tree as a connected acyclic graph and use the fact that a tree on n vertices has n-1 edges.

concepts.name: Euler circuits and trails
concepts.summary: Apply the degree conditions to decide whether a connected graph has an Euler circuit or trail and construct one.

concepts.name: Subgraphs and complete graphs
concepts.summary: Identify subgraphs and use the count n(n-1)/2 for the edges of a complete graph.

misconceptions.text: BFS and DFS visit vertices in the same order, so either one can be used for any purpose.
An adjacency matrix is always the better representation because lookup is constant time.
An Euler circuit visits every vertex exactly once.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm
concepts.summary: Run Dijkstra with a priority queue on a graph with nonnegative weights and recover the shortest path tree.

concepts.name: Minimum spanning trees
concepts.summary: Compute a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm and justify each edge choice.

concepts.name: Hamilton cycles
concepts.summary: Contrast Hamilton cycles with Euler circuits, use sufficient conditions such as Dirac's theorem, and explain why no simple degree test exists.

concepts.name: Bipartite graphs
concepts.summary: Test bipartiteness through BFS two-colouring or the absence of odd cycles.

concepts.name: Graph coloring basics
concepts.summary: Colour a graph properly, apply greedy colouring, and bound the chromatic number using cliques and maximum degree.

concepts.name: Topological ordering of DAGs
concepts.summary: Order the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so all edges point forward, using DFS finishing times or in-degree removal.

concepts.name: Complexity of graph traversals
concepts.summary: Analyse the running time of BFS, DFS and Dijkstra in terms of vertices and edges under each representation.

misconceptions.text: Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly with negative edge weights as long as there is no negative cycle.
A minimum spanning tree gives the shortest path between every pair of vertices.
A graph with all degrees even is guaranteed to have a Hamilton cycle.

concepts.name: Correctness of greedy graph algorithms
concepts.summary: Evaluate proofs of Prim, Kruskal and Dijkstra using the cut property and invariants about settled vertices.

concepts.name: Planar graphs and Euler's formula
concepts.summary: Use V-E+F=2 to derive edge bounds and show that K5 and K3,3 are nonplanar.

concepts.name: Kuratowski and planarity testing
concepts.summary: Judge planarity by finding subdivisions or minors of K5 or K3,3 and relate it to the four colour theorem.

concepts.name: Maximum flow and Ford-Fulkerson
concepts.summary: Model a capacitated network, find a maximum flow with augmenting paths in a residual graph, and track flow conservation.

concepts.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
concepts.summary: Evaluate a flow's optimality by exhibiting a cut of equal capacity and explain why the two values coincide.

concepts.name: Bipartite matching and Hall's theorem
concepts.summary: Find maximum matchings via augmenting paths or flow reduction and decide perfect matchings with Hall's condition.

concepts.name: Shortest paths with negative weights
concepts.summary: Choose among Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall and Dijkstra and detect negative cycles.

misconceptions.text: Greedily pushing flow along any path without ever undoing flow yields a maximum flow.
A graph is planar only if it contains no K5 as a subgraph, with no need to consider subdivisions.
A maximal matching, one that cannot be extended by adding an edge, is always a maximum matching.

concepts.name: Reductions to flow and matching
concepts.summary: Design reductions of problems such as project selection, edge-disjoint paths and assignment to max flow or matching.

concepts.name: Weighted matching and assignment
concepts.summary: Evaluate and select algorithms for minimum-cost perfect matching and min-cost flow, using dual potentials.

concepts.name: NP-hardness of graph problems
concepts.summary: Assess why Hamilton cycle, 3-colouring, clique and vertex cover are NP-complete and what that implies for algorithm choice.

concepts.name: Approximation and heuristics for graphs
concepts.summary: Design and justify approximation or heuristic algorithms, such as the MST-based metric TSP 2-approximation, with guarantees.

concepts.name: Strongly connected components
concepts.summary: Evaluate linear-time SCC algorithms and use the condensation DAG to structure analysis of directed graphs.

concepts.name: Treewidth and structural parameters
concepts.summary: Judge when bounded treewidth or other structure makes NP-hard graph problems tractable through dynamic programming.

concepts.name: Extremal and probabilistic graph arguments
concepts.summary: Construct proofs using extremal bounds, Ramsey-type arguments or the probabilistic method to show existence of graph structures.

misconceptions.text: Because Hamilton cycle is NP-complete, no algorithm can solve it on any realistic instance.
Approximation algorithms for NP-hard graph problems give optimal answers on small inputs.
Min-cost flow cannot be solved in polynomial time because it generalises shortest paths and flows.
